sections.html: Keeping this species is not too much of a problem as long as the water is kept clean and not too alkaline, with a pH of between 6.0 and 7.0. They like a planted aquarium where they hide during the day. Also provide pipework for this genus for a choice of hiding places.

In its native habitat it feeds on small invertebrates and crustaceans. In the aquarium it will eat anything offered, such as frozen bloodworm, catfish tablets, white worm (sparingly), prawns and shrimp.

The sexes can be distinguished best by the shape of the maxillary barbels: curved in males, straight in females. Mature males also have a modified anal fin, similar to that of other species in this family.

Mees (1974) assigned this species to Tatia but Ferraris (2007) reverted it to the original genus Centromochlus. In September 2019, following earlier work by U.K. aquarist and amateur ichthyologist Steven Grant (2015), a paper by Bárbara B. Calegari et al. reclassified this species, Tatia carolae Vari & Ferraris, 2013 and C. macracanthus Soares-Porto, 2000 into a new genus, Balroglanis. It is still found in some online searches as Centromochlus akwe.

Description: Centromochlus (Balroglanis) akwe differs from other Centromochlinae by having a vermiculated colour pattern on the dorsum. It is diagnosed from other Centromochlus by having the pectoral-fin spine with dark bars alternating with light bars.

Etymology: Balroglanis means "Balrog Catfish", derived from the Balrog Durin's Bane in J. R. R. Tolkien's Lord of the Rings legendarium. The specific name akwe is named for the Akwê (Xerente) indigenous people who previously inhabited the middle and upper Tocantins River basin (Tocantins, Brazil), where this catfish occurs.
